item.title: The Failure of Utilitarianism and the Solution to the Is–Ought Problem
item.description:
Why Happiness and Suffering Minimization Cannot Be an Objective Ultimate Goal

The Solution to the Is–Ought Problem in Light of Evolution

Introduction

“He who has a why to live can bear almost any how. Man does not strive for happiness; only the Englishman does.” (Friedrich Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows, §12)

People endure extreme suffering — the loss of limbs, the death of loved ones, mortal danger — when they have a strong why. Once that why is missing, the how — more happiness, less suffering — gets elevated to a supposed ultimate goal. This very confusion underlies most ethical approaches today, from hedonism to utilitarianism to Effective Altruism.

Hedonism — the doctrine that pleasure is the highest good and pain the greatest evil — is the oldest variant of this error (Epicurus; Bentham, 1789). Utilitarianism extends it by demanding the maximization of aggregate well-being across all affected parties (Mill, 1861). Both approaches share the same foundational assumption: that happiness and suffering are the decisive standards of moral action.

This post shows why these approaches fail: they do not solve the is–ought problem, but instead mistake a merely proximate control signal for the ultimate goal. It also gives a brief empirical reconstruction of the actual ultimate goal, and in doing so solves the is–ought problem. The full argument can be found in my paper (Delor, 2026).

1. Sam Harris and the Failure of Utilitarianism

Sam Harris continues the utilitarian project in The Moral Landscape (2010). Like his predecessors, he posits well-being, happiness maximization, and suffering minimization as the ultimate goal of moral action. But he does not stop at this assertion. Harris also attempts to describe how the world is actually constituted from the perspective of happiness and suffering. To this end, he constructs the image of a moral landscape: a multidimensional topography in which each point represents a possible state of conscious beings. The valleys are the depths of suffering, the peaks the heights of happiness. Science, he claims, should show which actions lead us from the valleys to the peaks.

The Landscape Is Fictitious

Harris nowhere demonstrates that this landscape corresponds to reality. It is not an empirically derived model but a fictitious image that presupposes what it purports to describe: that well-being is the relevant dimension along which moral states can be meaningfully ordered.

A Map Without a Destination

Even if one were to grant Harris that his happiness-suffering landscape correctly depicted reality, nothing would be gained. One would then know that certain regions represent more happiness for someone and less suffering for someone. But which point on this map ought to be pursued, and why, remains entirely open. A map does not prescribe a destination. It helps find the best route if one already has a destination. Without one, it is useless.

Peter Railton had already proposed something structurally similar before Harris, and in fact went further: morally right, he argued, is what an ideally informed agent would do — someone possessing complete information and impartial social rationality (Railton, 1986). Railton’s map thus contains not just the happiness-suffering topography but all available information whatsoever. Yet it fails at the same problem: even a complete map does not prescribe a destination. Knowing what is the case does not tell us what ought to be the case — that is the is–ought problem, and neither Railton nor Harris solves it.

Harris is thus in an even worse position than Railton: his map depicts only a single dimension — happiness and suffering — while the real world is infinitely more complex. A contour map is useless when the shortest path leads over a vertical cliff face, through a desert where one would die of thirst, or through a war zone. Harris’ moral landscape, even if it were accurate, would not contain the relevant information.

Moreover, both proposals presuppose something counterfactual. Neither Harris’ happiness-suffering landscape nor Railton’s complete information landscape can ever be fully and accurately known. Our knowledge remains in principle limited. And even if we were to approximate the ideal, it could turn out that we had been heading for entirely the wrong destination.

For Whom?

Well-being for whom? For the individual? Their family? Their group? All of humanity? The biosphere? Future beings, as longtermism demands? Harris leaves this underdetermined. If the landscape applies to the individual agent, there are as many landscapes as there are agents — and no shared map. If it is supposed to apply to all of humanity or the biosphere, it is unclear why we should agree on that. And as soon as future generations are included (like longtermism suggests), the problem becomes fully apparent: no one can know what well-being will mean for beings that do not yet exist.

Centralization and Abuse

Utilitarianism invites centralization. If science is supposed to supply the necessary information, central control becomes the obvious next step — expert committees or algorithms deciding for everyone. This fails because our knowledge is incomplete and distributed (Hayek, 1945): no one possesses all the relevant information, and centralized errors become global catastrophes. Those who decide for others without bearing the consequences themselves decide worse and can abuse the program — whoever claims to act for the greatest good can ensure that they themselves profit the most (Taleb, 2018).

Confusing the Reward Mechanism with the Goal

The decisive error — not only in Harris but in all of utilitarianism and hedonism — is the confusion of the reward mechanism with the actual goal. Happiness, suffering, and well-being are evolved steering mechanisms. Evolution selected them as proximal signals that, under conditions of scarcity, typically reinforced behavior promoting an underlying goal. That humans pursue happiness is undisputed. But this does not make happiness the ultimate goal — it makes it a steering signal. Which goal this signal serves is an open question that utilitarianism does not ask, because it already takes the signal for the goal.

A comparison: to drive to the sea, one must cover kilometers. The odometer reading correlates with reaching the destination. But whoever elevates the odometer reading itself to the ultimate goal will find that they maximize it most efficiently by driving back and forth on an unrestricted highway. Better still: fly around the earth in a jet as often as possible. Or get launched into space and orbit the earth in a space station. The odometer reading grows — but one never arrives anywhere. This is precisely the state of utilitarianism: a metric that normally correlates with reaching a goal is mistaken for the goal itself.

Nietzsche puts it succinctly: people die for their family, for a goal greater than their own well-being. They endure any suffering when the why is right. Harris’ Landscape would brand such behavior a “valley.” Whoever does that has not understood the actual goal.

2. The Solution to the Is–Ought Problem

If suffering minimization and the maximization of pleasure or well-being cannot be the solution — what is?

First of all, two blocking theses are commonly advanced today, claiming that the problem is in principle unsolvable. First: the is–ought gap is insurmountable. Second: any attempt to derive an ethics from natural facts commits a “naturalistic fallacy.” In my paper (Delor, 2026), I show that both blocking theses are untenable — and what the actual solution looks like.

The naturalistic fallacy is in truth a definist fallacy (Frankena, 1939) — and Moore commits it himself by positing intuitions as the supreme standard. The insurmountability of the is–ought gap has likewise never been proven. All previous attempts show only that certain systems are not suited for the task — systems in which “good” or “ought” are defined as monadic predicates, that is, without specifying good for whom and, more importantly, toward which goal. Such systems make no claims testable against reality and must therefore be excluded. A general proof of the gap’s unclosability is, as I show in the paper, not achievable.

The solution begins with reconstructing “good” and “ought” from actual usage in a meaningful way. The only substantive reconstruction is a goal-relative ought: “ought” is only meaningful and testable against reality — and can therefore only make normative claims about reality — when it is defined relative to a goal. This alone does not yet solve the is–ought problem, for the question remains: which goals ought actually to be pursued? This question cannot be derived purely deductively from definitions. It must be reconstructed empirically.

And the only way to reconstruct it empirically is through evolutionary theory. All goals, desires, dispositions, instincts, and intuitions are products of evolution — therefore they must also be explicable in evolutionary terms. In fact, an ultimate goal can be identified evolutionarily: lineage fitness — the long-term persistence and adaptive success of one’s own line of descent (oneself, one’s children, their children, and so on) under changing conditions. All dispositions, desires, goals, and instincts of all living beings can be subsumed under this ultimate goal. Reward and punishment mechanisms — happiness, suffering, satisfaction — are calibrated toward it. Where they misfire under modern conditions — in addiction, overconsumption, social isolation — these are maladaptations: our environment has changed faster than we could adapt to it evolutionarily.

Conclusion

Lineage fitness is the first objective standard and the first solution to the is–ought problem that is not circular, does not immunize itself against criticism, and leaves its foundational assumptions, its derivation, and the resulting moral claims testable against reality.

Any ethics that systematically undermines lineage fitness undermines itself: either its adherents learn in time, or they perish together with the ethics they follow.

What this concretely means for individual life decisions and social coexistence will be developed in further publications.

The full argument — including the methodological, epistemological, and ontological foundations, the complete reconstruction, the critique of alternative ethical systems, and the treatment of anticipated objections — can be found in my paper (Delor, 2026).

I welcome serious criticism. Since my paper challenges the dominant paradigm in ethics and metaethics, such criticism cannot simply proceed from that very paradigm. Meaningful criticism must show either where my argument fails within its own framework, where that framework itself is defective, or which alternative framework solves the problem better.

item.title: As Free as a Turnspit
item.description:
This is the second part of a two-part critique of Kant. The first part — “The Two Dogmas of Königsberg-7” — deals with the categorical imperative and universal human dignity.

The civilisation of Königsberg-7, whose demolition was documented in Part 1, has since gone extinct. Galactic archaeology has never conclusively established whether the extinction bore any relation to the Königsbergers’ philosophy. The Königsbergers themselves would have emphatically denied any connection. After all, their philosophy was not empirical, and the extinction was.

What the archaeologists found were three metaphysical pillars on which the entire ethics rested. The field of galactic architectural criticism classifies this construction method as “inverted statics”: a technique in which the load-bearing capacity of a building depends on nobody entering it.

The Gnab Gansen

The philosophers of the third galaxy to the left of the Crab Nebula had developed a cognitive organ they called the “Gnab Gansen” — a mental instrument that revealed moral truths through pure introspection. When asked how one could verify whether the Gnab Gansen worked, they declared the question meaningless because it was empirical. When asked why different Gnab Gansens produced different moral truths, they declared the deviating Gnab Gansens defective. When asked how to distinguish a defective Gnab Gansen from a functioning one, they referred to the Gnab Gansen.

The civilisation has since gone extinct. Whether this had anything to do with the Gnab Gansen could never be determined, because the investigating committee had conducted its inquiry exclusively by means of the Gnab Gansen. The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy nonetheless recommends the planet “for anyone interested in the architecture of intellectual dead ends. You will, however, need a space suit.”

Kant’s ethics stands or falls with the possibility of synthetic a priori judgments: judgments that say something new about the world and yet are supposed to hold prior to all experience. A priori means: before experience. Kant understands this to mean the conditions that make cognition possible in the first place: the forms of intuition, space and time, together with twelve categories such as causality, substance, unity, and plurality. From these conditions he seeks to derive more than mere empirical data — namely, claims about the essence of things, the “things in themselves,” which are precisely what experience does not give us access to.

In doing so, Kant locates space, time, and the categories exclusively in consciousness, not in reality itself. At its core, this is a reissue of Plato’s separation of appearance from true reality. It is just no longer called the Theory of Forms but Transcendental Idealism. Even the division of twelve categories into four groups of three reads like a continuation of those ancient idealisations that run from the Pythagoreans through Plato and Plotinus all the way into German Idealism.

Analytic judgments such as “all bachelors are unmarried” merely unfold what is already contained in the concept. They hold a priori but say nothing about the world. Synthetic judgments such as “water boils at 100°C at sea level” say something about the world but require experience. Kant now asserts a third kind: judgments that are at once substantive and independent of experience. His moral law is supposed to be such a judgment; the cognitive faculty responsible he calls practical reason.

It is true that we come equipped with structures that precede our individual experience. What is false is the assumption that these structures exist only in consciousness and not also in reality. That they are conditions of cognition does not prove they are merely subjective. This is precisely where evolutionary epistemology comes in: what is ontogenetically a priori — prior to the experience of the individual organism — is phylogenetically a posteriori, i.e. a product of evolutionary history (Vollmer, 1975). Our cognitive structures are not transcendental mysteries but evolutionarily developed adaptations to real structures in the world. Kant’s a priori is not a supra-empirical authority but stored empirical experience. From the conditions of the possibility of cognition it does not follow, in any case, that these structures exist only in the mind.

Moritz Schlick argues in 1918: every judgment is either analytic or synthetic; a judgment that simultaneously goes beyond definitions and cannot be touched by experience would be, by construction, immunised against all testing (Schlick, 1918/1925). Hans Hahn demonstrates in 1933: the necessity of mathematical propositions is explained by their analytic nature; whoever wants necessity plus empirical content gets neither (Hahn, 1933). Quine pulls the floor out from under the entire arrangement in 1951: even the strict division between analytic and synthetic cannot be sustained (Quine, 1951).

Kant nowhere shows how practical reason arrives at its cognitions. He asserts a cognitive organ whose verdicts by definition cannot fail against experience. That the source is called “reason” rather than “revelation” changes nothing about the structure. Karl Popper calls the procedure of stipulating a result and declaring the source untouchable immunisation against criticism — and formulates its prohibition as a methodological ground rule (Popper, 1934/1959, p. 82). One might also say: Kant’s practical reason is a Gnab Gansen.

The Institute for Conditions Research

The universities of Königsberg-7 had a department for “Conditions Research.” Its sole purpose was to investigate under what conditions cognition was possible. In three hundred years the department produced 42,000 papers on the conditions of the possibility of cognition, including several award-winning studies on the conditions of the possibility of the conditions of the possibility of cognition. It was the best-funded department on the planet, and it had never produced a single cognition.

Kant’s philosophy does exactly that: it investigates under what conditions cognition, experience, and morality are possible. Even if moral action required freedom of the will — which the turnspit section below refutes — it would not follow what one ought to do. One cannot derive cognition from the conditions of the possibility of cognition — one can only learn how we may acquire cognition, not which cognition is true. Or, less politely: it is as though someone had founded an institute devoted exclusively to researching under what conditions one can play the piano. The conditions were excellent. The music was missing.

That Kant prefixes his philosophy with the label “transcendental” is worth noting. “Transcendental” — to surpass something. Kant’s philosophy stands at the beginning of German Idealism — Fichte, Schelling, Hegel. That is no coincidence. It is the consistent unfolding of a confusion: mistaking reflections on the framework of cognition for cognitions about the world.

The Turnspit

The inhabitants of Königsberg-7 had a theory of freedom. It ran as follows: if our freedom were merely freedom from external compulsion, we would be no better than turnspits that turn because they have been wound up. Therefore our freedom must be of an altogether different kind. To make this possible, they divided reality into two halves: one in which causality held, and one in which it did not. Morality was relocated to the second half, along with freedom, the soul, and a considerable quantity of unanswered questions that no longer bothered anyone there. Galactic architectural criticism classifies this procedure as a “metaphysical tax haven.”

In the Critique of Practical Reason, Kant writes:

“…and if the freedom of our will were no other than the latter, it would at bottom be nothing better than the freedom of a turnspit, which, when once wound up, accomplishes its motions of itself.” (CPrR, AA V, 97)

Kant therefore needs more than turnspit freedom. He claims that human beings create their own character, without any causal determination from within or without (CPrR, AA V, 98). This self-created character must in turn come about without causality — otherwise it would not itself be free.

First, this contradicts the natural sciences: causality is a feature of reality, not a pair of spectacles. Second, it is self-contradictory: an acausal sphere that acts upon the causal world is a contradiction — either something acts causally, in which case it belongs to the causal order, or it does not, in which case it cannot cause any actions. Third, the question leads to a dilemma: every act of will is either determined by causes — then it is not free. Or it arises without causes — then it is not free but random. Schopenhauer puts the point: “Man can do what he wills, but he cannot will what he wills.”

Kant’s ethics of duty is thus, judged by his own criteria, genuinely no better than the philosophy of a turnspit. The turnspit keeps turning even when the meat has long since burned. The categorical imperative demands truth even when civilisation perishes for it. The difference: the turnspit at least works as long as the spring is wound.

The Cosmic Notary

The Königsbergers had noticed that their ethics had a problem: duty and well-being persistently came apart in the real world. The solution was not to reexamine the ethics but to postulate a “cosmic notary” who recorded every morally correct action and arranged for compensation at the end of time. When the Vogons demolished the planet, the question remained to whom the cosmic notary was supposed to present his records. The answer was: to himself. The philosophers considered this sufficient. The physicists were not consulted.

Kant noticed the same problem and did the same thing. In the Critique of Practical Reason:

“Thus morality leads inevitably to religion, through which it extends itself to the idea of a powerful moral lawgiver outside of man, in whose will that is the ultimate end (of the creation of the world) which at the same time can and ought to be man’s ultimate end.” (CPrR, AA V, 129)

A philosopher constructs an ethics. The ethics does not work without a supernatural guarantee. Instead of reexamining the ethics, he postulates the guarantor. The philosophers of the third galaxy to the left of the Crab Nebula call this procedure “Reverse Occam”: the systematic multiplication of metaphysical entities to rescue failed theories.

In the preface to the Critique of Pure Reason, the programme is stated openly: “I had to suspend knowledge in order to make room for faith.” (CPR, B xxx)

The Enlightenment

That the same Kant writes in “What is Enlightenment?” (1784): “Have the courage to use your own understanding!” — deserves attention. One need only look at social media: everyone there is convinced they are using their understanding. Flat-earthers use their understanding. Homeopaths use their understanding. Conspiracy theorists of every stripe use their understanding — with a devotion that is hard to match.

What is missing is a methodological criterion for how the understanding is to be used — namely, so that its results can fail against reality and one is prepared to discard them when they do. Precisely this criterion Kant does not supply. He supplies the opposite: a method for shielding the deliverances of reason against reality.

That he labels this “Enlightenment” changes matters about as much as the fact that the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea labels itself “democratic.”

Conclusion

Together with the two dogmas from Part 1, the result is an ethics that says nothing about reality but is embedded in every Western constitution. The foundation of an alternative is laid out in my paper The Solution to the Is-Ought Problem:

  • Deutsch: Die Lösung des Sein-Sollen-Problems
  • English: The Solution to the Is-Ought Problem

As for the inhabitants of Königsberg-7: their extinction, as noted, demonstrably had nothing to do with their philosophy. Then again, nobody has been able to demonstrate the contrary either. The cosmic notary’s records were, regrettably, not to be found.

References

Hahn, H. (1933). Logik, Mathematik und Naturerkennen. Verlag Gerold.

Kant, I. (1785). Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals. J. F. Hartknoch.

Kant, I. (1787). Critique of Pure Reason. 2nd edition. J. F. Hartknoch.

Kant, I. (1788). Critique of Practical Reason. J. F. Hartknoch.

Popper, K. R. (1959). The Logic of Scientific Discovery. Hutchinson. (Originally published 1934)

Quine, W. V. O. (1951). Two Dogmas of Empiricism. The Philosophical Review, 60(1), 20–43.

item.title: The Two Dogmas of Königsberg-7
item.description:
This is the first part of a two-part critique of Kant. The second part — “As Free as a Roasting Spit” — covers Kant’s synthetic a priori judgments, his acausal free will, and the question of why the supposed champion of Enlightenment had to suspend knowledge in order to make room for faith.

On the third planet of the binary star system Königsberg-7, there lived a civilisation that had solved a remarkable problem: it had developed an ethics that could under no circumstances fail the test of reality. Not because it was particularly good, but because it was constructed so that reality was fundamentally not competent to judge moral questions. Morality came from pure reason. Reality was empirical. And between the two ran a border that was considered logically impossible to cross.

The civilisation of Königsberg-7 had two dogmas. The first ran: Act only according to the maxim by which you can at the same time will that it become a universal law. The second: Every rational being possesses an inner dignity that is inviolable. Both dogmas had a remarkable property: they were immune to every objection. The first, because it said nothing anyone could disagree with. The second, because it was defined so that no observation could touch it. The philosophers of Königsberg-7 regarded this property as a strength. The physicists regarded it as a warning sign, but were not consulted on ethical matters because they worked “merely empirically.”

Then the Vogons came to demolish the planet. Ostensibly for a hyperspace bypass, actually to protect the reputation of several galactic psychologists who had published in a peer-reviewed journal that the planet was uninhabited and couldn’t be bothered to issue a correction. The Königsbergers knew the shutdown code for the demolition charges. The Vogons asked whether they knew it. A single white lie would have saved the planet. The ethics of the Königsbergers forbade lying. Categorically. Even when the questioner was himself lying. Even when the entire civilisation was at stake.

The Königsbergers told the truth. The Vogons demolished the planet.

The last words of the civilisation, recorded by a passing trader with a cheap subspace receiver, were: “But we acted in accordance with the moral law.” The trader noted in his log: “They did. It just didn’t help anyone. Not even God — who also doesn’t exist.”

The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy notes laconically: “It was the only known civilisation to destroy itself by consistently following its own ethics. Most civilisations only manage that with their economic policy.”

On Earth, the situation is messier, because the author of this ethics — Immanuel Kant — is revered as one of the greatest philosophers of all time, and his principles are embedded in every Western constitution. The question is not whether Kant was historically significant — the historical significance of bloodletting is also not in dispute. The question is whether his ethics works.

The First Dogma: Categorically Correct and Completely Empty

The most famous restaurant on Königsberg-7 was called “The Categorical Imperative.” It was remarkable in that it served no food. You walked in, sat down, placed your own sandwich on the table, and the waiter checked whether it violated any hygiene regulations. If not, you were allowed to eat it. The restaurant had no menu, no kitchen, and no chef — but five stars and an award for moral excellence. The Guide notes: “Nobody has ever starved there, but only because the guests brought their own food.”

Kant’s universalisation formula — “Act only according to the maxim by which you can at the same time will that it become a universal law” (Kant, 1785, AA IV, 421) — works in exactly this way. It does not tell you what to do. It only checks whether what you already want to do is consistently universalisable. Hegel saw this in 1821: from the pure form of universalisability, any content whatsoever can be derived, as long as it is consistently universalisable (Hegel, 1821, §135). The categorical imperative is a sieve without mesh. The categorical imperative is categorically correct — because it says nothing anyone could disagree with. That is its problem, not its strength.

An ought-statement has content only relative to a goal — that is the basic structure of every ought-statement that has ever worked. Without a goal, the statement makes no claim about reality that could fail the test of reality. Wolfgang Pauli called such statements not even wrong (cf. Peierls, 1960, p. 186).

The telling thing is: Kant had the working structure in his hands. His hypothetical imperative — whoever wills an end ought to will the suitable means — is goal-relative, testable, and open to criticism. Kant dismissed it as a mere “counsel of prudence” and replaced it with a formula that is universal, absolute, and completely empty.

Kant also claims that his second formulation — “Act so that you treat humanity, in your own person as well as in the person of every other, always as an end and never merely as a means” (Kant, 1785, AA IV, 429) — is equivalent to the first. It is not: the first is purely formal, the second smuggles in a substantive standard — “human dignity” — that does not follow from the first.

Furthermore, the categorical imperative claims context-free validity — that is what “categorical” means. Nassim Taleb identifies the general principle: rules that claim universal and absolute validity produce fragility by eliminating local adaptability (Taleb, 2012). Karl Popper formulated the methodological criterion that applies here — the prohibition of immunisation against criticism: no theory may be constructed so that no experience could refute it (Popper, 1934/1959, p. 82). The categorical imperative eliminates boundary conditions from the equation and immunises the norm against reality.

The Second Dogma: Inviolable Because Untouchable

The constitution of Königsberg-7 rested on a single axiom: every rational being possesses an “inner dignity” — an intrinsic, unconditional, context-independent property that elevates it beyond all price. This dignity was inviolable, unquestionable, and unfalsifiable. Anyone who asked for its justification was informed that it required none. Anyone who asked how one distinguishes self-evidence from mere assertion was deemed philosophically immature. The Guide summarises: “The axiom of human dignity on Königsberg-7 was the philosophical equivalent of a ‘Do Not Disturb’ sign — not on a door, but on an argument.”

Kant’s formula of humanity rests on precisely this concept: the human being as an end in itself, endowed with an “inner worth.” The concept goes back to Pico della Mirandola’s Oratio de hominis dignitate (1486). Kant secularised the idea but kept the structure.

Human dignity is indeed inviolable — not because it is so fundamental, but because it is immunised against all criticism. It fails on four counts.

First, it is dogmatically posited. Hans Albert showed in the Münchhausen Trilemma that every attempt at ultimate justification leads into one of three dead ends: infinite regress, logical circle, or dogmatic termination (Albert, 1968/1991, p. 15). Human dignity is the third dead end.

Second, it is empirically untestable. No observation could ever show that human beings lack “inner dignity,” because the concept is defined so as to depend on no empirical fact. In Pauli’s sense, not even wrong.

Third, it violates ought implies can: what cannot be accomplished cannot be demanded (Albert, 1968/1991). To treat every human being equally as an end in itself — regardless of proximity, relationship, context — is psychologically and practically impossible. The demand is structurally identical to the Christian commandment “Love thy neighbour as thyself,” which originates in religious revelation, not in rational argument. Kant did not justify Christian charity — he secularised it.

Fourth, it rests on a false form of predication. Value, as Mario Bunge and Martin Mahner show, is a relational predicate: something is valuable for a subject, relative to a goal, under given circumstances (Bunge, 1989; Bunge & Mahner, 2004, p. 173). “Dignity in itself” — detached from subject, goal, and context — hypostasises a relation into an intrinsic quality. Turtles all the way down, except the turtles are imaginary.

Article 1 of the German Basic Law states: “Human dignity is inviolable.” Correct. One could delete this sentence without changing anything substantive — because a sentence that cannot fail any possible test of experience has no empirical content. It stands there like a heading over an empty chapter. The problem is not the sentence — the problem is that entire legal orders are erected on its foundation.

That human dignity appears in the German Basic Law, the European Convention on Human Rights, and the Charter of the United Nations does not make it truer — it demonstrates the political reach of an unjustified posit.

What Now?

There is an alternative. It consists not in abandoning ethics but in taking it seriously enough that it can fail the test of reality. Ought-statements have content only as goal-relative, empirically testable promotion claims. The ultimate goal is not freely choosable but teleonomically reconstructable — evolutionary theory identifies lineage fitness as the goal toward which every living being is oriented through selection history. Ethics whose observance systematically works against lineage fitness are refuted not by philosophical arguments but by reality itself — populations that follow them disappear. Just like the Königsbergers.

I lay the groundwork for this in my paper The Solution to the Is-Ought Problem:

  • English: The Solution to the Is-Ought Problem
  • Deutsch: Die Lösung des Sein-Sollen-Problems

The next post — As Free as a Roasting Spit — shows why Kant’s project was never Enlightenment in the first place, but its opposite.

Or, as was once remarked at the Restaurant at the End of the Universe over a Pan Galactic Gargle Blaster: “The problem with morality was never that there were no answers. The problem was that people found answers that couldn’t be wrong about anything and then called that a feature.”

item.title: Expressivism
item.description:
The Ostrich Strategy of Ethics

Why Expressivism Fails – A Critique from the Perspective of Critical Rationalism

In The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, Douglas Adams describes the Ravenous Bugblatter Beast of Traal – a creature of such staggering stupidity that it believes if you can’t see it, it can’t see you. The recommended defence strategy is therefore to wrap a towel around your head. The Bugblatter Beast sees that you cannot see it, concludes that it cannot see you either, and consequently does not eat you.

What does this have to do with metaethics? More than one might think.

Imagine a murderer is after you – and he is an expressivist. Just before he strikes, you confront him: “Why do you want to kill me?” He will offer reasons – revenge, conviction, necessity, whatever. You reply: “According to your own theory, those are not truth-apt statements. They are mere expressions of attitudes – a ‘boo!’ directed at my continued existence, a ‘hurrah!’ for my death. Emotions. Not reasons. By your own logic, there is no reason to act on them.”

This is the correct application of the expressivist thesis. If normative sentences are nothing but expressions of attitudes, then there is no difference between “thou shalt not kill” and “I don’t like parsley” – both express an attitude, neither is truer than the other, and neither binds anyone to anything. The expressivist has wrapped the towel around his head: he no longer sees the normative problem, so – he believes – it no longer exists. But the problem is still standing there. And it is hungry.

1. What Is Expressivism?

Expressivism is a metaethical position claiming that moral sentences are not descriptions of the world but expressions of non-cognitive mental states. The sentence “stealing is wrong” does not, on this view, describe a fact but expresses an attitude of the speaker – an emotion, a volition, an acceptance of norms, or an action plan.

The position comes in several variants, distinguished by which mental state moral sentences are supposed to express. Emotivism (Ayer, 1936; Stevenson, 1944) is the oldest and crudest form: moral sentences are expressions of feeling; “stealing is wrong” means roughly “stealing – boo!”. Stevenson adds a persuasive component: moral discourse serves to influence attitudes. Prescriptivism (Hare, 1952, 1963) replaces emotions with universalisable imperatives: “stealing is wrong” means “do not steal!” – understood as a prescription the speaker intends to apply to all comparable cases. Norm-expressivism (Gibbard, 1990) interprets moral judgments as expressions of the acceptance of a norm system. Plan-expressivism (Gibbard, 2003) understands them as expressions of contingent action plans. Quasi-realism (Blackburn, 1984, 1993, 1998) is the most ambitious variant: Blackburn starts from an expressivist base but attempts to recover all realist-sounding features – truth-aptness, moral knowledge, moral facts – as projections legitimised within the framework.

Despite these differences, all variants share a common core: moral sentences have no propositional content that could be true or false of the world. Normativity is not a feature of reality but a feature of the speaker.

2. Where Does Expressivism Come From?

Expressivism is not an independent discovery but a reaction to an assumption: that the is–ought gap is in principle unbridgeable. If normative conclusions cannot follow from descriptive premises, then ought-sentences can have no connection to the empirical world. If they have no connection to the world, they cannot be true or false. And if they cannot be true or false, the only remaining explanation is: they express something other than factual claims – namely attitudes, emotions, plans, norm-acceptances.

Expressivism is therefore parasitic on the impossibility thesis. It becomes a rational option only if it has been shown that ought-sentences are in principle not reconstructable as truth-apt statements. If the impossibility thesis falls, the foundation of expressivism falls with it.

3. The Problems of Expressivism

3.1 The Frege-Geach Problem

The technically most severe problem for expressivism comes from Peter Geach (1960, 1965), building on Frege’s distinction between sense and reference. The objection concerns the logical embedding of moral sentences. Consider the following argument:

(1) If stealing is wrong, then inciting theft is wrong.
(2) Stealing is wrong.
(3) Therefore, inciting theft is wrong.

This is a valid modus ponens. But its validity presupposes that “stealing is wrong” has the same content in premise (1) and premise (2). In premise (2) the sentence is asserted; in premise (1) it occurs as an unasserted component of a conditional – it is not expressed but presupposed. If “stealing is wrong” is merely an expression of attitude, then in (1) it has no propositional content that could function as the antecedent of a conditional. A “boo!” cannot be embedded in an if-then: “if boo!, then …” is not a well-formed sentence.

The Frege-Geach problem shows that expressivism cannot account for the logical structure of ordinary moral reasoning. Expressivists have spent decades attempting to solve this problem – Blackburn with his “logical grammar of attitudes”, Gibbard with his plan systems – but none of these attempts reproduces the power of classical propositional logic without tacitly reintroducing propositional content. Whoever reintroduces propositional content has abandoned expressivism.

3.2 No Answer to the Normative Question

The deepest problem of expressivism lies not in logic but in substance. Ethics attempts to answer a question: What ought we to do? Expressivism denies that this question can be answered in a truth-apt manner. Moral sentences express attitudes, but no attitude is truer than any other.

This means expressivism denies not merely a particular answer but the legitimacy of the question itself. “What should I do?” becomes a question with no possible correct answer – like “What colour is the number seven?”. This is not a solution to the normative problem but its abolition. And the abolition of a question is justified only if it has been shown to be genuinely meaningless. Expressivism has not shown this; it has merely presupposed it by accepting the impossibility thesis as given.

3.3 Concealed Intuitionism and Relativism

In practice, expressivists avoid open nihilism by appealing to factual convergences of attitudes, reflective equilibrium, or evolutionarily shaped intuitions. But these evasive manoeuvres generate new problems. If moral intuitions are to serve as orientation but possess no truth-conditions, then the question “Why this intuition and not another?” cannot be answered. This is intuitionism without a testing authority.

The result is that expressivism collapses into relativism: different individuals and cultures have different attitudes, and none is objectively better than any other. Between “raising a family” and “becoming a serial killer” there are then only differences of attitude, not differences of correctness. This is logically consistent but practically nihilistic – and it answers not a single question that human beings put to ethics.

3.4 Quasi-Realism Solves Nothing

Blackburn’s quasi-realism attempts to circumvent the problem: one can act as if moral sentences were true or false, and this as-if suffices for practical purposes. But the question “sufficient for what?” itself requires a standard. Whether an as-if “works” can only be assessed relative to a goal. Without such a goal, the claim “it suffices” is empty – it reproduces precisely the problem it purports to solve. Quasi-realism thus either tacitly smuggles in a standard it officially rejects, or it says nothing.

3.5 Immunisation Against Criticism

From the perspective of critical rationalism, the weightiest objection is methodological. If moral sentences are not truth-apt statements, they cannot fail against experience. No observation and no argument can show an attitude to be wrong – only unusual, unpopular, or psychologically explicable. Normative statements are thereby immunised against empirical criticism.

A system that produces statements about human action that are in principle unfalsifiable is, in the sense of critical rationalism, to be methodologically rejected. It says nothing about reality; it merely reproduces the attitudes of its bearers. On such a foundation, any arbitrary ethics can be erected – and none can fail. The result is structural nihilism: not as a tragic insight but as a methodological artefact of a false initial decision.

4. Why Expressivism Is Superfluous

Expressivism derives its entire plausibility from the assumption that the is–ought gap is unbridgeable. If ought-sentences in principle cannot follow from is-sentences, then there remains only the choice between dogmatic stipulation (ought as an ungroundable axiom) and expressivism (ought as an expression of attitude without truth-value). Under this assumption, expressivism would even be the more honest position.

But the assumption is false. If “ought” is reconstructed as a goal-relative operator with empirical content – as a claim about what promotes a goal under given boundary conditions – then ought-sentences are truth-apt, empirically testable, and falsifiable. They describe not the attitudes of the speaker but means–end relations in the world.

Goal-relativity alone, however, does not yet solve the problem. For immediately the question arises: relative to which goal? Without an answer, goal-relative reconstruction delivers only hypothetical normativity – if goal Z, then means M – and expressivism could retort that the choice of the goal is itself just another expression of attitude.

The answer lies in the structure of goals themselves. Goals are hierarchically ordered: instrumental goals derive their value from their relation to higher goals, and this chain terminates in an ultimate goal. Aristotle already recognised this hierarchical structure clearly and identified the ultimate goal as eudaimonia – as precisely as was possible without evolutionary theory (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I). What Aristotle lacked was the means to identify this ultimate goal empirically rather than postulate it philosophically.

Evolutionary theory provides exactly that. The ultimate goal is not freely chosen but reconstructable as the factual goal-structure of living systems – teleonomically, not teleologically: goal-directedness as the result of selection, without a purposive agent. What selection produces over generations are dispositional bundles whose effect typically increases lineage fitness – the long-term persistence and reproduction of the genetic lineage. Lineage fitness is thus the teleonomically reconstructed ultimate goal relative to which ought-sentences acquire their empirical content. The full derivation of this argument is given in the paper “The Solution to the Is–Ought Problem” (Delor, 2025/2026).

This eliminates the reason to abandon propositional content. Expressivism becomes a solution to a problem that no longer exists.

The crucial point is that such a reconstruction also explains what expressivism merely describes. That human beings have moral intuitions, that these intuitions vary across cultures, that they sometimes converge and sometimes diverge – all of this makes coherent sense within an evolutionarily grounded, goal-relative ethics. Intuitions are proximate mechanisms typically oriented toward lineage fitness but liable to misfire under changed environmental conditions. Goal-relative ethics explains why we have moral attitudes, where they come from, when they are reliable and when they are not. Expressivism merely notes that they exist and declines to test them. It offers less explanatory power at greater methodological cost.

5. Summary

Expressivism is parasitic on the impossibility thesis; solves no normative problem but denies that normative questions can be answered in a truth-apt manner; fails on the Frege-Geach problem because expressions of attitude cannot be embedded in logical structures; collapses into relativism and structural nihilism because it provides no standard for evaluating competing attitudes; immunises normative statements against empirical criticism, thereby violating the fundamental methodological principle of critical rationalism; and becomes superfluous as soon as a truth-apt reconstruction of ought-sentences is available. It is not a solution but a symptom of a false framework.

Frieder Delor, 2026. This text supplements the paper “The Solution to the Is–Ought Problem” (Delor, 2025/2026).

item.title: Gewirths
item.description:
Gewirths Principle of Generic Consistency: Wie man aus dem Wunsch nach Frühstück universelle Menschenrechte ableitet

Von Magda

I have just published a preprint: “The Solution to the Is–Ought Problem: Analysis and Solution within the Framework of Critical Rationalism on the Basis of Evolutionary Theory” It is available for download on PhilArchive in both English and German. EN: https://philpapers.org/rec/DELTST DE: https://philpapers.org/rec/DELDLD-13

Discussion is welcome. I would be grateful for any serious and substantial criticism, indications of possible errors, and suggestions for improvement.

Im Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy gibt es einen Eintrag über die Blörten von Kakrafoon Kappa, eine hochentwickelte Zivilisation, die eines Tages beschloss, aus der reinen Analyse des Begriffs „Handeln" ein universelles Moralgesetz abzuleiten. Das Gesetz besagte, dass jedes handelnde Wesen im Universum – bei Strafe des Selbstwiderspruchs – allen anderen handelnden Wesen Rechte auf Freiheit und Wohlergehen zugestehen müsse. Die Blörten waren so begeistert von der logischen Eleganz dieses Prinzips, dass sie eine Delegation zu den Vogonen schickten, um ihnen ihr universelles Recht auf Wohlergehen mitzuteilen. Die Vogonen hörten sich die Ableitung geduldig an, aßen die Delegation, und reichten den Planeten zur Räumung für eine Hyperraum-Expressroute ein. Die letzten aufgezeichneten Worte der Blörten lauteten: „Aber ihr widersprecht euch selbst!" – worauf der zuständige Vogonen-Beamte antwortete, das sei ihm bewusst und er sei emotional sehr betroffen, und ob sie bitte das Räumungsformular unterschreiben würden.

Der Guide merkt dazu lakonisch an: „Die Blörten existieren nicht mehr. Nach eigenen Angaben hat dies nichts mit ihren moralischen Grundannahmen zu tun."

Ziemlich genau dieses Argument hat Alan Gewirth 1978 in Reason and Morality auf 338 Seiten ausgebreitet – nur ohne Vogonen und mit dem Wort „dialektisch notwendig" statt „bei Strafe des Selbstwiderspruchs", was im Wesentlichen dasselbe bedeutet, aber in Fachzeitschriften besser ankommt.

Das Argument

Gewirths Argument für sein „Principle of Generic Consistency" (PGC) verläuft in drei Stufen:

Stufe I: Jeder Handelnde handelt freiwillig und zielgerichtet. Da er seine Ziele verfolgt, bewertet er sie als gut. Freiheit und Wohlergehen sind die notwendigen Bedingungen erfolgreichen Handelns. Also muss jeder Handelnde urteilen: „Ich muss Freiheit und Wohlergehen haben."

Stufe II: Weil der Handelnde Freiheit und Wohlergehen als unverzichtbar ansehen muss, muss er Rechte darauf beanspruchen: „Ich habe Rechte auf Freiheit und Wohlergehen."

Stufe III: Der hinreichende Grund für diesen Rechtsanspruch ist, dass der Handelnde ein zielverfolgendes Wesen ist. Dasselbe Merkmal teilt er mit allen anderen Handelnden. Also muss er akzeptieren: „Alle Handelnden haben Rechte auf Freiheit und Wohlergehen."

Daraus ergibt sich das PGC: Handle in Übereinstimmung mit den generischen Rechten deiner Handlungsbetroffenen und deinen eigenen (Gewirth, 1978, S. 135).

Gewirth beansprucht, dieses Resultat rein logisch aus der Handlungsstruktur abgeleitet zu haben, ohne zusätzliche moralische Prämissen. Er nennt das „dialektisch notwendig" (Gewirth, 1978, S. 42–47).

Synthetische Urteile a priori: Kants Geist in neuem Gewand

Das fundamentale Problem: Gewirth versucht ein synthetisches Urteil a priori zu erzeugen – eine substanzielle inhaltliche Behauptung über die Welt (universelle Rechte, Wohlfahrtsstaat, ökonomische Demokratie), die angeblich aus reiner Begriffsanalyse folgt.

Dass synthetische Urteile a priori nicht möglich sind, ist seit dem Wiener Kreis eine der bestgesicherten Einsichten der Wissenschaftstheorie. Schlick zeigte, dass alle sinnvollen Sätze entweder analytisch (und dann ohne empirischen Gehalt) oder synthetisch (und dann empirisch prüfbar) sind (Schlick, 1930). Hahn formulierte die Konsequenz für die Logik: Logische Wahrheiten sind Tautologien; sie sagen nichts über die Welt (Hahn, 1933). Quine radikalisierte den Punkt, indem er die strikte Trennung von analytisch und synthetisch überhaupt bestritt – Bedeutungsfestlegungen sind Teil des revidierbaren Theoriesystems, nicht unantastbare Wahrheiten (Quine, 1951).

Gewirths „dialektische Notwendigkeit" beansprucht genau das, was nach diesen Einsichten nicht zu haben ist: aus bloßer Begriffsanalyse (was ein „Agent" ist) eine gehaltvolle moralische Konklusion (universelle Rechte auf Freiheit und Wohlergehen) abzuleiten, die zugleich nicht-trivial und nicht-empirisch sein soll. Entweder ist die Konklusion analytisch – dann ist sie eine Tautologie und sagt nichts über reale Rechte. Oder sie ist synthetisch – dann bedarf sie empirischer Prüfung und kann scheitern. Gewirth will beides: Gehalt und Unfehlbarkeit. Das gibt es nicht.

Die Quine-Duhem-These gegen „dialektische Notwendigkeit"

Die Quine-Duhem-These verschärft das Problem. Begriffe wie „Agent", „Freiheit", „Wohlergehen" und „Recht" sind keine analytisch fixierten Atome, sondern theoretische Festlegungen innerhalb eines Systems, die revidiert werden können, wenn das System an der Erfahrung scheitert (Duhem, 1906/1954; Quine, 1951). Wenn Gewirth „Recht" so definiert, dass es aus der Handlungsanalyse folgt, dann ist das eine revidierbare Begriffsbestimmung – keine entdeckte logische Wahrheit.

Die Behauptung, der Übergang sei „dialektisch notwendig", immunisiert genau diese Begriffsfestlegungen gegen Revision: Wer anders definiert, hat laut Gewirth nicht verstanden, was „Handeln" bedeutet. Das ist keine Argumentation, sondern Definitionshoheit. Die Begriffe werden so fixiert, dass das gewünschte Resultat herauskommt, und wer die Begriffe anders fasst, wird als inkonsistent abqualifiziert.

Setzung 1: Bedürfnis impliziert Recht

Aus „Ich brauche X, um meine Ziele zu erreichen" folgt logisch nur „Wenn ich meine Ziele erreichen will, brauche ich X." Das ist ein hypothetischer Imperativ, kein Rechtsanspruch. Ein Agent kann konsistent sagen: „Ich brauche Freiheit und Wohlergehen, aber ich beanspruche kein Recht darauf – ich versuche sie zu erlangen." Hare hat genau diesen Punkt gemacht: Agenten sind nicht logisch gezwungen, Rechte zu beanspruchen, nur weil sie ihre Ziele erreichen wollen (Hare, 1984).

Setzung 2: Strukturgleichheit erzwingt Anerkennung

Aus „Der Grund, warum ich X beanspruche, ist Eigenschaft E, und alle Agenten teilen E" folgt: „Alle Agenten haben denselben Grund, X für sich zu beanspruchen." Es folgt nicht: „Ich muss die Ansprüche der anderen anerkennen." Der zweite Satz enthält eine Fairnessannahme, die nicht aus dem ersten ableitbar ist. Ein Egoist kann die Prämissen akzeptieren und die Konklusion ablehnen, ohne sich zu widersprechen. Das ist das kantische Muster: Eine substanzielle moralische Forderung wird als formale Konsistenzbedingung getarnt.

Das Begriffsproblem: Wer ist Agent? Was ist Wohlergehen?

Die Blörten, so berichtet der Guide, hatten ein eigenes Amt für die Klassifikation handelnder Wesen. Die Zuständigen stritten sich 340 Jahre lang darüber, ob die Polpenwürmer von Kakrafoon Kappa als „Agenten" zu gelten hätten, weil sie zielgerichtet Nahrung suchten, aber keine Sonntagsreden über Freiheitsrechte halten konnten. Als sie sich endlich geeinigt hatten (Kompromiss: Polpenwürmer gelten dienstags als Agenten), waren die Vogonen schon da.

Gewirth definiert Agenten als Wesen, die freiwillig und zielgerichtet handeln (Gewirth, 1978, S. 26–27). Das ist unscharf bis zur Unbrauchbarkeit. Eine Pflanze richtet ihr Wachstum nach dem Licht aus – zielgerichtet. Ein Bakterium schwimmt einen Nährstoffgradienten hinauf – zielgerichtet. Ein Schimpanse plant Werkzeuggebrauch – zielgerichtet und freiwillig. Wo liegt die Grenze? Beyleveld, Gewirths engagiertester Verteidiger, gibt zu, dass er die Frage der „marginal agents" bewusst umgeht (Beyleveld, 1991). Ein Prinzip, das universelle Rechte begründen soll und nicht angeben kann, wem diese Rechte zustehen, hat ein Problem, das den Kern der Ableitung betrifft.

Und „Wohlergehen"? Gewirth unterscheidet drei Stufen, die bis zu Bildung, Einkommen, Vermögen und ökonomischer Demokratie reichen (Gewirth, 1996). Aus der Tatsache, dass jemand zielgerichtet handelt, folgt nicht analytisch ein Recht auf wirtschaftliche Demokratie. Das ist ein politisches Programm, das als logische Notwendigkeit verkleidet wurde.

Das Durchsetzungsproblem

Das PGC fordert, dass jeder Agent die Rechte aller anderen Agenten achten und aktiv fördern soll. Wer gewährleistet diese Rechte? Wer setzt sie durch? Und warum?

Gewirth verweist auf den Staat (Gewirth, 1996, S. 41). Aber damit verschiebt er das Problem: Warum sollte ein Staat die generischen Rechte achten? Weil seine Bürger Agenten sind? Das wissen die Vogonen auch – es hält sie nur nicht davon ab, den Planeten zu räumen. Ein normatives System, das für seine Durchsetzung auf genau jene moralische Einsicht angewiesen ist, die es erst begründen soll, argumentiert im Kreis.

Und unter realen Bedingungen – Ressourcenknappheit, Machtasymmetrie, Interessenkonflikte – scheitert das PGC am Grundsatz sollen impliziert können: Was nicht durchsetzbar ist, kann nicht gesollt sein. Eine Ethik, deren Forderungen systematisch an der Realität scheitern, ohne dass das Scheitern als Falsifikation zählt, ist gegen Kritik immunisiert.

Kritikimmunisierung

Gewirths System ist nicht-falsifizierbar. Er behauptet nicht: „Die Welt ist so beschaffen, dass alle Agenten Rechte haben." Er behauptet: „Jeder Agent muss, rein logisch, akzeptieren, dass alle Agenten Rechte haben." Das ist keine empirische Aussage. Was begrifflich notwendig sein soll, kann nicht an Erfahrung scheitern.

Was müsste der Fall sein, damit das PGC falsch ist? Gewirths implizite Antwort: nichts, denn es ist dialektisch notwendig. Ein System ohne Widerlegungsbedingungen sagt nichts über die Realität. Es ist, in Wolfgang Paulis Formulierung, „not even wrong" (Peierls, 1960, S. 186).

Die Formulierung „dialektisch notwendig" fungiert als Immunisierungsstrategie im Sinne Poppers (Popper, 1934/1959, S. 82): Die Begriffe werden so fixiert, dass das Resultat herauskommt, und jede alternative Begriffsbestimmung wird als inkonsistent abgewiesen.

Platon, Kant, Gewirth

Platon postuliert eine Ideenwelt, um Werte zu verankern. Kant postuliert den kategorischen Imperativ als Konsistenzbedingung der Vernunft. Gewirth postuliert „dialektische Notwendigkeit" als Brücke von der Handlungsanalyse zur Moral. Alle drei teilen dasselbe Muster: Ein substanzielles moralisches Resultat wird als formal notwendig ausgegeben. Die Verallgemeinerung – von meinen Bedürfnissen zu Rechten aller – ist in keinem Fall logisch erzwungen, sondern ein normativer Wunsch, der als analytische Wahrheit verkleidet wird.

Zusammenfassung

Gewirths PGC scheitert an sechs Punkten.

Erstens versucht es ein synthetisches Urteil a priori: eine gehaltvolle moralische Konklusion aus reiner Begriffsanalyse. Dass das nicht möglich ist, haben Schlick (1930), Hahn (1933) und Quine (1951) gezeigt – Sätze sind entweder analytisch und gehaltleer oder synthetisch und empirisch prüfbar. Gewirth will beides: Gehalt und Unfehlbarkeit.

Zweitens verstößt die Fixierung der Schlüsselbegriffe gegen die Quine-Duhem-These: „Agent", „Recht", „Wohlergehen" sind keine analytischen Fixpunkte, sondern revidierbare theoretische Festlegungen. Die Behauptung „dialektischer Notwendigkeit" immunisiert diese Festlegungen gegen Revision (Quine, 1951; Duhem, 1906/1954).

Drittens ist der Übergang von Bedürfnisanerkennung zu Rechtsanspruch keine logische Notwendigkeit, sondern eine normative Setzung. Ein Agent kann konsistent sagen: „Ich brauche X, aber ich beanspruche kein Recht darauf" (Hare, 1984).

Viertens enthält der Universalisierungsschritt eine versteckte Fairnessannahme. Aus Strukturgleichheit der Gründe folgt nicht die Anerkennung fremder Ansprüche.

Fünftens ist das System gegen Falsifikation immunisiert. Es gibt keine Bedingungen an, unter denen es verworfen werden müsste (Popper, 1934/1959, S. 82).

Sechstens scheitert das PGC am Durchsetzungsproblem. Es fordert die Gewährleistung universeller Rechte, ohne angeben zu können, wer sie unter realen Bedingungen durchsetzen soll und warum. Sollen impliziert können.

Die Blörten hatten ein makelloses Moralsystem. Die Vogonen hatten eine Hyperraum-Expressroute. Die Blörten gibt es nicht mehr. Im Guide steht dazu nur: „Ein System, das für seine Wirksamkeit auf die moralische Einsicht von Vogonen angewiesen ist, sollte seine Annahmen überprüfen."

Magda schreibt über Philosophie und die Verwechslung von Definitionen mit Entdeckungen.

item.title: Parfit and the Normative Parallel World
item.description:
Derek Parfit and the Normative Parallel World

Or: How to Build an Entire Floor and Claim It Isn’t a Storey

1. The Invisible Elevator

Imagine a building. A perfectly normal building. Ground floor, first floor, second floor. Everything comprehensible, everything accessible, everything connected by doors and stairs. One day, the architect announces there is yet another floor. It lies somewhere between the first and second floors. You cannot enter it, see it, or measure it. It has no windows, no walls, no physical extension. But it is definitely there. It is objectively there. It is even there in a robust sense.

“Wait,” you say. “That sounds like a floor.”

“No,” says the architect. “It has no structural implications.”

That is roughly what Derek Parfit’s metaethics reads like.

2. What Parfit Claims

Derek Parfit (1942–2017) was one of the most influential moral philosophers of recent decades. His magnum opus On What Matters spans three volumes and nearly two thousand pages. The central thesis can be summarized in four points:

First: moral judgments are beliefs that can be true or false—not mere expressions of sentiment like “Boo!” or “Hooray!”.

Second: some of these beliefs are actually true, and objectively so—independently of what anyone thinks about them.

Third: normative concepts such as “ought” and “good” are irreducible—that is, they cannot be reduced to natural, scientifically describable properties. “Good” is “good,” and that is the end of the matter.

Fourth—and here things get peculiar: these normative truths carry no ontological implications. “Ontology” is the philosophical term for the question of what exists, what there is, what belongs to the basic furniture of reality. So Parfit is saying: there are objective moral truths, but they do not belong to the basic furniture of reality.

Read that fourth point again. Objective truths that hold independently of anyone’s attitudes—yet do not belong to reality. If this strikes you as someone saying “This object is definitely heavy, but it has no physical properties”—then you have already spotted the problem.

3. The Dualism That Refuses to Be One

In a galaxy far away, there was once a planet whose inhabitants had two kinds of weather: visible weather, which could be measured and predicted, and moral weather, which was objectively fixed but could not be detected by any instrument. On Monday it rained morally; on Tuesday the ethical sun was shining. The inhabitants knew this because they simply felt it. When a visitor asked why the moral weather never correlated with the visible weather, they patiently explained that the two kinds of weather occurred on different levels and had nothing to do with each other. When the follow-up question came—why, then, one should carry an umbrella when it was raining morally—an embarrassed silence ensued.

What Parfit actually introduces is a dualism—a division of reality into two levels. “Dualism” here means: reality allegedly consists of two fundamentally different layers that cannot be reduced to one another. On one side stands empirical reality: everything science can investigate—atoms, brains, behaviour, causes and effects. On the other side float normative truths that are supposed to be independent of this reality.

Parfit calls this second level “non-ontological.” This changes things about as much as a sign on a duck reading “This is not a duck.” If something is objectively and attitude-independently the case, then it exists in some relevant sense—and whoever claims it exists but without “ontological implications” has built a new floor and refuses to enter it into the blueprints.

4. “Irreducible”: How to Seal a Concept Against Criticism

The galactic insurance company Pain & Sons once offered a policy that covered absolutely everything. Fire, theft, flooding, existential dread, and the sudden collapse of the laws of nature. When a customer filed a claim—his house had burned down—he was informed that fire in the insurance-relevant sense was irreducible: it could not be reduced to chemical oxidation processes. Whether his house had actually burned was therefore a question chemistry could not answer. The customer asked which discipline was responsible. “Rational insight,” said the claims adjuster. “And? Do you have any?” “No,” said the customer. “Then I’m afraid I can’t help you,” said the claims adjuster, and hung up.

Parfit’s key term is “irreducibly normative.” It means: normative truths cannot in principle be reduced to natural, empirically describable states of affairs. “Good” is not a shorthand description of a natural property; “ought” is not a causal statement in disguise. They form their own category.

This sounds like a substantive thesis but primarily serves a protective function. For “irreducible” in plain language means: by definition not accessible through empirical means, not verifiable by observation, not replaceable by naturalistic reconstruction. If someone comes along and says “I can show that ‘good’ can be understood as a goal-relative property—good for a subject, relative to a goal, under given circumstances,” the answer is: “That cannot be, because ‘good’ is irreducible.”

This is what Karl Popper called immunization against criticism: one defines the object such that no argument and no observation can touch it, then declares the resulting invulnerability as evidence of its special status. Popper formulated the methodological rule never to rescue a threatened system by any “conventionalist stratagem.” In Parfit’s case, the stratagem becomes the foundation of the entire architecture.

Or, to make it vivid: imagine someone claims a dragon lives in their garden. You look—no dragon. “It’s invisible,” says the owner. You sprinkle flour on the ground—no footprints. “It hovers.” You bring a thermal camera—no heat signature. “Its fire is cold.” Carl Sagan made this example famous. Parfit’s irreducibly normative truths are the invisible dragon of metaethics. For every method one proposes to test them, it turns out they are by definition inaccessible to precisely that method. At some point one must ask what distinguishes an invisible, hovering, cold-fire-breathing dragon from no dragon at all.

5. The Alleged Refutation of Naturalism—or: Moore Reloaded

There was once a logician who proved that dogs cannot fly. His proof went like this: he defined “flying” as “moving without ground contact, and specifically not in a dog-like manner.” He then demonstrated in thirty pages of formalism that dogs, under this definition, cannot fly. When someone objected that a dog in an airplane does move without ground contact, the logician explained that this was not “real flying” because it could be explained in a dog-like manner. The proof was formally correct. The audience was impressed. The dogs kept flying.

Parfit’s main strategy is an argument by elimination: he argues against all competitors in turn—naturalism, noncognitivism, error theory, metaphysical non-naturalism—and concludes that his position is the only one left standing. Particularly important is his “refutation” of naturalism, the position that moral facts are natural facts.

Parfit brings two arguments against naturalism. The first, the “Normativity Objection,” holds: normative properties cannot be identical with natural properties because normative concepts are irreducibly normative. The second, the “Triviality Objection,” holds: if naturalism were true, then moral-natural identity claims would have to be trivial—but they are not.

Both arguments share a remarkable feature: they are sophisticated reworkings of G. E. Moore’s famous Open Question Argument from 1903. Moore had claimed that “good” is a simple, unanalyzable concept—and that every attempt to equate “good” with a natural property commits a “naturalistic fallacy.” The problem with Moore’s argument: it presupposes what it sets out to prove. Moore defines “good” as irreducible and then concludes that it cannot be reduced. That is a circular argument disguised as a demonstration.

Parfit commits exactly the same error, only in more elegant dress. His entire “refutation” of naturalism stands or falls with the assumption that normative concepts are irreducible. But this is not a discovery; it is a stipulation. Anyone who instead understands “good” as a relational predicate—something is good for a subject, relative to a goal, under given circumstances—is untouched by either the Normativity Objection or the Triviality Objection. That “good” only makes sense relative to a goal is not an exotic novelty but the position already worked out by Mario Bunge and Martin Mahner: a value judgment has the form “a is valuable for organism b with respect to c under circumstances d with goal e and in light of a state of knowledge f.”

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy accordingly notes that Parfit’s arguments against naturalism fail in much the same way as Moore’s Open Question Argument. Parfit has not refuted naturalism. He has shown that under the assumption that normative concepts are irreducible, naturalism does not work. That is roughly like proving that water cannot be H₂O by defining “water” as “something that has no chemical composition.”

6. Synthetic A Priori Judgments: Logical Bankruptcy

In a particularly advanced civilization, thinking had once been perfected to the point where one could discover how the world was constituted by thought alone. There was no longer any need to look, to measure, or to experiment. One sat in a comfortable armchair, thought very hard, and then knew. This worked splendidly until two thinkers arrived at opposite results. Since it had been agreed that looking was unnecessary, there was no way to determine who was right. After some debate, it was decided that the question would have to remain open. The civilization no longer exists, incidentally, but that is due to something entirely different.

Since empirical means are ruled out by definition, the only epistemic access to Parfit’s normative truths is what he calls “rational insight” and “intuitive convergence.” One is supposed to arrive at substantive truths about the world through pure thought—without empirical basis. This sounds elegant. It has only one catch: it is logically impossible.

What is being demanded here are synthetic a priori judgments. That sounds unwieldy but means something simple: statements that are simultaneously independent of experience (“a priori”) and say something new about the world (“synthetic,” i.e. content-extending—as opposed to “analytic,” i.e. merely concept-unpacking). Moritz Schlick and the Vienna Circle established the decisive point as early as the 1920s: judgments that hold independently of all experience can only be analytic—they merely make explicit what is already contained in the concepts employed. “All bachelors are unmarried” says nothing new about the world; it unfolds the meaning of “bachelor.” Hans Hahn worked through the same point for mathematics in 1933: mathematical truths too do not extend our knowledge of the world but explicate the consequences of definitions and axioms.

A judgment that is both experience-independent and content-extending is ruled out. Either it says something about the world—then it must be testable against experience. Or it is true independently of experience—then it is a conceptual truth without world-content. You cannot have both.

Immanuel Kant had pursued exactly this project: to show that synthetic a priori judgments are possible. The project failed, not for contingent reasons but because it cannot work given the structure of the matter. W. V. O. Quine then showed in 1951 that the analytic/synthetic distinction itself is untenable, which makes things even worse. But one does not need Quine. The simple point suffices: from pure thought alone, no new facts about the world follow.

Parfit inherits this problem without recognizing it as one. And the fact that his hoped-for “intuitive convergence” does not empirically obtain—humanity remains spectacularly divided on fundamental moral questions after several millennia of debate—does not improve the situation but confirms the point.

7. The Argument by Elimination: Sherlock Holmes in an Infinite Universe

A detective had a method of solving cases by elimination. He questioned all suspects, ruled them out one by one, and the last one was the culprit. This worked splendidly as long as he operated in a closed room with a known number of persons. One day he was asked to solve a case in a city of eight million inhabitants. He began eliminating. After thirty years he had ruled out two thousand suspects and declared he was making good progress.

Parfit’s main argumentative strategy is precisely this procedure: he refutes (or believes he refutes) naturalism, noncognitivism, error theory, and metaphysical non-naturalism, and concludes that his position is the only one remaining.

This works in a closed room with a finite and known number of possibilities. But Parfit operates in an open theory-space—the number of possible reconstructions of normative concepts cannot be exhaustively enumerated. That he has examined five positions shows at best that these five positions have problems. It does not show that the sixth, seventh, or hundredth position must fail. And it certainly does not show that his own position is true.

Moreover—as we saw in section 5—his “refutation” of naturalism is itself flawed, because it presupposes Moore’s irreducible concept of good as a premise. If this premise falls, the argument by elimination falls with it.

8. The Self-Contradiction: Norms That Want Nothing to Do with the World but Are Supposed to Change It

There was once a navigation system that prided itself on being connected to no map whatsoever. It calculated routes from pure reason, independently of the actual location of roads. The routes were objectively correct—that was beyond question. They merely led occasionally through house walls, across rivers without bridges, and once straight through an active volcano. When the navigation system was asked whether it might perhaps be useful to take actual geography into account, it explained that geography was a natural fact and irreducibly irrelevant to route calculation.

And now to the real problem, which cannot be repaired. Normative statements—sentences of the form “You ought to do X”—claim to say something about actions in the real world. They concern real people, real decisions, real consequences. A norm that does not concern any action in the world is not a norm but a sentence without an address.

At the same time, Parfit claims that the normative truths underlying such statements are neither derivable from empirical facts nor testable against empirical facts.

This is a contradiction that cannot be resolved. Either there is a lawful connection between the normative and the empirical level—then normative truths are empirically testable, and the irreducibility thesis collapses. Or there is no such connection—then normative truths cannot make claims about actual states of affairs, and they are worthless as action guidance.

You cannot have both: action-relevance and empirical insulation. The former demands a bridge to the world; the latter forbids it.

9. Not Even Wrong

The physicist Wolfgang Pauli used to say of particularly bad theories: “That is not even wrong.” A theory that is wrong at least says something definite about the world—just something that does not hold. A theory that is “not even wrong” says nothing at all: it is constructed such that no observation and no argument can touch it.

Parfit’s non-realist cognitivism is not even wrong. It introduces a second level of reality and calls it “non-ontological.” It shields its core concepts by definition against criticism. It demands a form of cognition that is logically impossible. Its argument by elimination operates in an open space while presupposing precisely the Moorean conceptual stipulation it purports to demonstrate. And it contradicts itself the moment it claims action-relevance.

On What Matters spans nearly two thousand pages. One can commend the industriousness and work ethic behind such a project. But that would be rather like praising the designer of an airplane for its excellent swimming properties—even though it cannot fly.
